rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all six peaks and identify critical pairs while limiting run time. The high final organic fraction reduces the risk of missing strongly retained compounds.

Injection 1 already reached the maximum CRF of 1.000. Shorten the gradient while keeping composition and temperature fixed to seek a faster fully resolved method, using the substantial resolution margin.
Shorten the gradient another grid step to reduce analysis time while preserving the maximum CRF. The current minimum resolution of 2.68 provides room to test further compression.
Test the shortest permitted gradient to locate the speed limit at fixed composition and temperature. The first pair may fall below R = 1.5; injection 3 remains a fully resolved, maximum-CRF fallback.

Test whether higher temperature changes selectivity enough to resolve the first pair at the shortest gradient. This isolates temperature effects; injection 3 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Higher temperature worsened the critical separations, so test the lowest temperature at the same short gradient to assess whether selectivity improves. Injection 3 remains the fastest confirmed method with CRF 1.000.

Reduce the gradient slope to improve the first pair from R = 1.39 toward full resolution while retaining the shortest programmed gradient. The final hold should still elute the last compound quickly, potentially giving a faster maximum-CRF method than injection 3.

Shift the gradient window upward while preserving its slope to accelerate the last peak without strongly compressing the critical first pair. Injection 7 provides a fully resolved fallback if the higher starting organic fraction reduces early resolution too much.

Shift both organic endpoints upward one grid step, preserving the slope that resolved every pair in injection 8. This should accelerate the last peak while testing whether the earliest pair retains its resolution margin.

Continue shifting the gradient window upward at constant slope to reduce last-peak retention while preserving full resolution. This reaches the maximum final organic fraction; injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step while retaining the strongest endpoint and shortest gradient. This tests further acceleration of the last peak while checking that early elution does not compromise the first pair.

Raise temperature one grid step to shorten retention, using the improved minimum resolution of 1.77 as a margin. This tests whether a modest temperature increase preserves CRF 1.000 despite the selectivity loss seen at higher temperatures.

Increase the starting organic fraction one step to seek faster elution at the current temperature. The shallower gradient may help resolution, but the earliest peaks are near the dead-time region, so this run tests the onset of early-pair compression.

Return to the starting fraction that preserved early resolution and test one higher temperature step to establish the thermal speed limit. If the first pair falls below 1.5, injection 12 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Test whether cooling restores the early-pair separation lost at the higher starting organic fraction in injection 13. This completes the nearby composition–temperature boundary check while retaining injection 12 as the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Reduce the gradient slope to try to restore the critical first pair at 35 C, where R was 1.36 with a 0.95 endpoint. This tests a warmer, narrower-window alternative while retaining injection 12 as the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Lower the starting organic fraction to retain the first pair longer and test whether it regains gradient-dependent separation at 35 C. Injection 16 showed that reducing slope alone had little effect when those peaks eluted near the gradient onset.

Lower the endpoint one grid step to give the first pair the modest additional separation needed from R = 1.42. This tests a fully resolved warmer alternative; injection 12 remains the fastest confirmed method with maximum CRF.

Refine around injection 12 by lowering the endpoint one step, testing whether a slightly shallower gradient improves the critical-pair margin with little time cost. Injection 18 is borderline despite its rounded CRF, so the confirmed R = 1.58 method remains preferable.

Cool injection 19 by one grid step to test a short, maximum-CRF alternative with a larger critical-pair resolution margin. Injection 12 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method; this run assesses the resolution–time tradeoff nearby.

Test a lower starting organic fraction near the fastest confirmed method, keeping the early pair farther from the pre-gradient elution region. This should offer another short, fully resolved option; injection 12 remains the speed benchmark.

Lower the endpoint one step from injection 21 to increase its narrow first-pair resolution margin while keeping a short analysis time. This refines a less aggressive starting composition; injection 12 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Cool injection 21 one step to improve its critical-pair margin while retaining a strong endpoint for rapid final elution. This refines the short-method alternatives without repeating a run; injection 12 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved choice.

Back off from the failed 35 C condition in injection 16 by one temperature step to seek full resolution in this narrower gradient window. Injection 12 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method, with the last peak at 2.58 min.

Use the final injection to test a larger resolution margin by cooling injection 24 one grid step, with all peaks expected well before 10 min. Injection 12 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method and already achieves the maximum CRF of 1.000.
